text_post: I decided to go spend a few days in vacation there, what a mistake. There seldom truly is anything to do, and anything is tame and artificial. The Geylang area, the city's Chinese district, is the closest thing to a ghetto, and even then it's just a bit disorderly but not more than Chinatown in any big Western town, and a few sex shops with dildos in Geylang are the closest thing to anything non Disneyesque you will find in the whole city state. Even the shopping centers don't have anything even remotely seedy, and the bookstores are empty and full of books to "maximize a child's development". My head hurts just to think about it. There are even government warnings to "behave well" everywhere. Even when you circulate on roads, there are electric panels that flash government reminders to "be nice". It is the worst of the British nanny state with the worst of Asian authoritarianism. The people are usually kind when you ask them for help, but they will very seldom volunteer helping you. Like Western society, it is a cold and individualist society. Women are cold and stuck-up and will largely ignore you (you are nothing special anyway as there are plenty of young Western expats living there). You might once in a blue moon find one who fancies Westerners, but in general, people in Singapore live them to make money and have a good career, not because they're particularly invested in the place they live in, and it shows. Most of the residents are ethnically Chinese, and Chinese people are in general orderly, but selfish, cold and rapacious. Constantly as I dealt with clerks who were ethnically Chinese, especially with the older generations, I was struck with how it seemed I was really bothering them and they wished I'd go away quickly. There is a minority of Indian people, and those generally are much nicer and more welcoming. There are also Malays but I didn't have much interaction with them. Something that is really telling is that when I went to the mall, in the line for a taxi, I had three taxi drivers in a row ignoring me and going away because my destination wasn't the specific area of town where I wanted to go! I can understand needing to make money... but come on, isn't a taxi driver supposed to help the public? I did notice however that the younger ethnically male Chinese who are more educated seem warmer and less cold and stern than the older ones, in general. Although most of them seem to be beta cucks extraordinaires. All in all Singapore is a beautiful and clean, and parts of it downtown look like they're straight out of the future, but there really is nothing exceptional to do here and people aren't particularly pleasing to deal with. If you like freedom, you will feel like a kid whose hand is being held over and over again. As I was in the Changi airport to head over to the Philippines and I heard OFWs talking about themselves, I was instantly struck by the difference. Filipinos in comparison are just so humble, warm, helpful and gentle. I much, much preferred my part of my vacation that was in the Philippines, to be sure. I'll take a place that is messier and dirtier and where people are blunter, but more honest, ANY day.

author: Fonduman
text_post: Hard to say. I'm LS, so I don't approach girls, so they seem more or less the same everywhere except for when you interact with them for other reasons. But Enginehead did most of the interacting with taxi drivers, cashiers etc, since it helps to know some Chinese with most of them.  I did get some stares, but I'm not sure if they were positive or negative lol. Even though Singapore isn't bad for an Asian country in terms of average height, I still felt a little like a giant there, so when you stand out it makes sense to get stares.  I think I only saw a very limited area of the city though, and we usually just stuck around shopping malls, things like that. Air conditioning, food. The food is pretty good. The transport is convenient and cheap - buses every two minutes, electronic payment system. Here, it's more like buses every half an hour, and you pay with cash still.  From what Enginehead has said, it seems like a decent place to visit, or maybe to live if you're rich, but I wouldn't want to be a typical person living there. There's no minimum wage, so many people work for slave-wages. The working culture is like Japan's, people expected to work 6 days a week standard, often 12 hours a day. People sound rude and ruthless, there was backstabbing everywhere Enginehead has worked there. Perhaps like any large city. Rents are high. There's a culture of elitism - sounds like the reputation of your school is of vital importance. Pollution is bad - particularly the haze due to forest fires in nearby countries. Some aspects of the economy are right wing, with all the associated perks - little social security, poor people not being able to afford healthcare, expensive education, etc.  One thing I remember Enginehead said about the dating culture, though, girls go for the 5 Cs - credit card, car, country club, and I don't remember the other two, but the jist of it comes down to materialism lol. Wouldn't surprise me if the girls there are generally hypergamous.  Quote:As far as I understand, you have lived in Northern Ireland with your Singaporean wife for around a year and a half to two years now? How is she adjusting? Three years in February.  Well, there isn't a great deal to adjust to. Other than the weather. She still thinks it's cold when I don't sometimes, but other than that I think she's just glad to be away from the perpetual Singaporean steamroom lol.  Culturally, she says people are much friendlier here. Also, her work environment is healthier - management is fairer, reasonable hours, better pay, sick days, etc. I don't think there's much in the way of difference between cultures that are important, really. Big cities tend to have a western culture by default - maintain personal space, be polite, etc. It's not like China where they'll see no issue in telling you how fat you are, which is quite different to the west. I guess it helps that we don't take ourselves too seriously here, it's not like we're easy to offend.
